name: What we left behind: parachutes, backshells and heat shields
short_status: Twelve landing sites carry entry hardware identified from orbit, almost all by HiRISE: heat shields, backshells, parachutes, descent stages and Curiosity's tungsten ballast. At the oldest the pieces are only likely.
page_title: What we left behind: parachutes, backshells and heat shields

facts.label: Viking 1 (1976)
facts.value: HiRISE imaged the Chryse Planitia site on 22 November 2006. The 3-metre lander was precisely located and likely positions were found for the heat shield, the backshell and the parachute attached to it. The lander fix was confirmed by overlaying topographic contours derived from the lander's own pictures onto the orbital image, which HiRISE reports as an excellent match. Note the hedge: everything other than the lander is described as likely or candidate. None of it is confirmed.

facts.label: Viking 2 (1976)
facts.value: HiRISE imaged the Utopia Planitia site on 21 November 2006. The lander was precisely located and likely positions were found for the heat shield and backshell. That image was accidentally smeared in places when the high-gain antenna restarted tracking during the very short exposure, which HiRISE says was the first such unintentional smear after hundreds of pictures.

facts.label: Mars Pathfinder (1997)
facts.value: Imaged 21 December 2006. The lander is visible with its ramps, science deck and airbag remnants; the backshell and parachute lie to the south; and four features were identified as possible pieces of the heat shield. HiRISE's own caption revises the Pathfinder-era interpretation: a bright glint that the 1997 team took for the backshell is now thought more likely to be insulating material from the inside of the heat shield, because the backshell and parachute were actually hidden behind a ridge from the lander's viewpoint.

facts.label: Spirit (2004)
facts.value: Imaged 22 November 2006 at Gusev Crater. The parachute shows as a bright irregular patch with wrinkles and folds in the fabric clearly visible; the cone-shaped backshell nearby "appears relatively undamaged by its impact with the martian surface", in the words of the HiRISE caption written by Steve Squyres; the heat shield remnant is a separate, damaged object; and the lander sits near the small crater the team named Sleepy Hollow. A 2012 follow-up frame, ESP_028070_1655, was released under the title Spirit Lander Backshell Heatshield and Parachute.

facts.label: Opportunity (2004)
facts.value: The first colour HiRISE view of the site, taken 10 April 2017, shows the lander as a dark centre amid reddish airbags at the bottom of Eagle Crater, the crumpled parachute still attached to the bluish backshell, and the heat shield crash site. The parachute has visibly blown around in the wind, leaving an arc of darker ground. Opportunity's rover tracks, by contrast, had been erased by wind within a decade.

facts.label: Phoenix (2008)
facts.value: The backshell with its parachute, the heat shield and the lander were all identified in Vastitas Borealis, but at 68 degrees north they vanish every winter. About 30 cm of carbon dioxide frost freezes onto the surface during the polar night, and in a January 2010 frame the hardware could not be picked out at all: the frost camouflaged it, and HiRISE noted that even after the frost sublimates, winter dust may keep the pieces hidden.

facts.label: Curiosity (2012)
facts.value: Four objects on the ground: the rover, the crashed descent stage, the heat shield, and the backshell with its parachute. A frame taken 17 August 2012, twelve days after landing, resolved seven bright spots around the descent stage crash that may be pieces of hardware, dark streaks radiating from the impact, and bright fragments scattered downrange of the backshell. The rover's own mast shadow is visible in the same image.

facts.label: Curiosity's tungsten ballast
facts.value: Ten minutes before reaching the atmosphere the entry vehicle separated from the cruise stage, and two minutes later it jettisoned two 75 kg tungsten blocks called cruise balance mass devices. A Context Camera image of the predicted impact area, about 80 km west of the landing site, found four large fresh impacts rather than two. HiRISE resolved craters 3 to 5 metres across in a strewn field at least 8 km long. The reading is that two impacts are the tungsten blocks and two are pieces of the cruise stage, which was far likelier to break up. The descent stage later released six more 25 kg tungsten blocks from low altitude, whose marks were imaged by the Context Camera.

facts.label: InSight (2018)
facts.value: Imaged 11 December 2018 in Elysium Planitia. The heat shield reads as a saturated bright spot, which HiRISE interpreted as a specular reflection from its dark outer face landing upward. The lander sits in a darkened patch where its thrusters disturbed the dust, with two bluish extensions that are the solar arrays. The backshell and attached parachute lie to the southwest; a dark streak running south past the parachute is probably a pre-existing dust devil track rather than anything InSight did.

facts.label: Perseverance (2021)
facts.value: HiRISE imaged the site on 19 February 2021, one day after landing, and caught four things in one frame: the rover in the blast pattern left by the descent stage, the descent stage's own V-shaped crash debris pointing back at the rover, the heat shield, and the parachute with the backshell. NASA's caption notes that the objects are highly visible now but will get dustier and slowly fade into the background over years.

facts.label: How big the parachutes are, and a published disagreement
facts.value: NASA's 2009 page on Curiosity's parachute describes a disk-gap-band canopy with 80 suspension lines, more than 50 metres long, opening to a diameter of nearly 16 metres (51 feet), and calls it the largest ever built to fly on an extraterrestrial mission. NASA's Mars 2020 landing page gives Perseverance's parachute as 70.5 feet (21.5 metres) in diameter, deploying about 240 seconds after entry at an altitude of about 11 km and a speed of about 1,512 km/h, and JPL's 2022 article on Ingenuity's survey of the wreck calls it the biggest ever deployed on Mars and counts 80 suspension lines on it. We found no NASA page that reconciles the two diameters or that states the two canopies differ in size.

facts.label: The backshell, up close
facts.value: On 19 April 2022, Ingenuity's 26th flight took ten aerial colour images of Perseverance's backshell and parachute at the request of the Mars Sample Return team. The backshell had hit the ground at about 126 km/h (78 mph) and stood upright with its protective coating apparently intact; many of the 80 suspension lines were visible and undamaged; about a third of the dust-covered orange and white canopy could be seen, with no sign of supersonic inflation damage. The flight lasted 159 seconds and covered 360 metres at 8 metres above the ground.

facts.label: The pieces that move
facts.value: Perseverance's parachute and backshell lie about 1 km northwest of its landing site, but fragments have travelled much further. By sol 508 (24 July 2022) the operations team had catalogued roughly half a dozen suspected pieces of entry hardware in Hogwallow Flats, about 2 km from the crash zones: shiny multi-layer insulation whose dot pattern matched the spacecraft's thermal blankets, Dacron netting, and shredded string. One blanket fragment was snagged on a rock and seen flapping in the breeze. NASA's assessment is that the wind carried them there over days or weeks.

facts.label: Tianwen-1 and Zhurong (2021)
facts.value: HiRISE imaged China's landing site in southern Utopia Planitia on 6 June 2021, three weeks after the 14 May landing. The frame shows the lander in its blast pattern, the Zhurong rover a little to the south after driving off, and both the parachute with its backshell and the heat shield lying separately on a smooth, largely boulder-free plain.

facts.label: Schiaparelli (2016)
facts.value: Schiaparelli's crash on 19 October 2016 left three things in Meridiani Planum: the lander module, which NASA reports hit at more than 300 km/h (more than 180 mph), the parachute with its back shell, released prematurely, and the heat shield, which had separated as planned. HiRISE's first colour view of the site was taken on 1 November 2016.

facts.label: Beagle 2 (2003, found 2015)
facts.value: Beagle 2, lost on Christmas Day 2003, was found in HiRISE imagery in a finding ESA announced on 16 January 2015. ESA's statement places the lander beside "the main parachute and what is thought to be the rear cover with its pilot/drogue parachute still attached close by". The hedge is ESA's own: the rear cover identification is not confirmed, which is the weakest link in the count of twelve sites.

facts.label: The debris as an instrument
facts.value: Landings blow bright dust away and leave dark blast zones, and HiRISE has monitored how those zones fade. Scientists expected the fading to follow a model that would predict when the marks vanish. A frame taken 28 February 2015, two and a half years after Curiosity landed, showed the opposite: the blast zones were not fading as fast as predicted and might even be darkening. In the same series the parachute can be seen flapping around in the wind near the backshell. HiRISE's own conclusion was that the processes moving dust around on Mars are not yet understood.

facts.label: How much is there
facts.value: The most-cited figure comes from Cagri Kilic of West Virginia University, writing in The Conversation on 20 September 2022: adding up the mass of all spacecraft ever sent to Mars gives about 9,979 kg, subtracting the 2,860 kg then still operating leaves 15,694 pounds (7,119 kg) of debris. He also cites the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs for 18 human-made objects delivered over 14 missions. Treat both numbers with care. They count spacecraft and leave out the aeroshells and parachutes that carried them: Curiosity's heat shield and back shell alone were 4.5 metres across. And the figure is stale, because InSight, Zhurong and Ingenuity have all stopped working since it was published, which on the same accounting moves their mass from the operating column to the debris column.

timeline: In 36 hours HiRISE images the Viking 2, Spirit and Viking 1 sites, locating the landers and finding likely heat shields, backshells and parachutes at all three. It is the first time 1976-era entry hardware is picked out from orbit.

HiRISE images the Gale Crater landing site 24 hours after Curiosity's arrival. The sky crane's impact scar shows dark streaks with small white dots in and beyond them, read as possible pieces of the crashed stage.
A less oblique frame at 27 cm per pixel resolves all four pieces of Curiosity hardware, seven bright spots at the descent stage crash, and debris downrange of the backshell.

HiRISE covers the impact field of Curiosity's two 75 kg tungsten cruise balance masses about 80 km west of the landing site, and finds four large craters, 3 to 5 metres across, in a strewn field at least 8 km long.

Following a Russian crowdsourced search led by Vitali Erogov (the spelling used on the HiRISE page; usually written Vitaly Egorov), HiRISE re-images candidate Mars 3 hardware in Ptolemaeus Crater: a bright 7.5-metre patch consistent with an 11-metre parachute, plus candidate heat shield, retrorocket and lander. The identification has never been confirmed. The same caption notes that Viking 1's parachute, on the ground since 1976, can still be seen from orbit as a bright area, which is part of why a 1971 parachute was thought plausible.

Two and a half years of monitoring show that the dark blast zones at Curiosity's landing site are not fading as models predicted and may be getting darker, and that the parachute is flapping in the wind.
HiRISE obtains the first colour view of the Schiaparelli crash site, showing the lander module, the prematurely released parachute and back shell, and the heat shield in three separate places.
HiRISE images InSight in Elysium Planitia with its heat shield glinting to the northeast and its backshell and parachute to the southwest.
One day after Perseverance lands, HiRISE captures the rover, the crashed descent stage, the heat shield and the parachute and backshell in a single frame in Jezero Crater.
HiRISE images China's Tianwen-1 lander, the Zhurong rover, and the mission's parachute, backshell and heat shield in southern Utopia Planitia.
Ingenuity's 26th flight photographs Perseverance's backshell and parachute from 8 metres above the ground, at the request of the Mars Sample Return team, and returns ten colour images.

NASA publishes a HiRISE frame taken on 13 June 2026 showing Perseverance as a green speck west of Jezero with its tracks behind it, the day before the rover passed a marathon of driving. Twenty years after it first catalogued Viking's parachutes, the same camera is still watching the hardware humans leave on Mars.

images.caption: HiRISE image of the Perseverance landing site in Jezero crater taken on 19 February 2021, one day after landing, with four objects labelled by the HiRISE team: the parachute and back shell at left, the crashed descent stage, the rover sitting in the pale blast pattern left by the hovering descent stage, and the heat shield at right.

Enlargement from the HiRISE image of the Viking 1 landing site in western Chryse Planitia taken on 22 November 2006, showing the bright object HiRISE identifies as the likely back shell with the parachute attached to it. For everything other than the lander itself, HiRISE uses the words likely or candidate, and those identifications remain unconfirmed.

Annotated cutout from the HiRISE image of the Spirit landing site in Gusev crater taken on 22 November 2006. Box a marks the parachute and the cone shaped back shell, box b the lander beside the crater the team named Sleepy Hollow, box c the damaged remnant of the heat shield, and box d Spirit itself, just southeast of the layered plateau the team named Home Plate.

The first colour HiRISE view of the Opportunity landing site in Meridiani Planum, taken on 10 April 2017. HiRISE reports the lander as a darker centre amid reddish airbag material at the bottom of Eagle crater, the crumpled parachute still attached to the bluish back shell, and an arc of darker ground where the parachute has been blown about by the wind.

Labelled HiRISE cutout of the InSight landing site in Elysium Planitia, imaged on 11 December 2018, marking the lander in the patch of dust disturbed by its thrusters, the back shell with its parachute, and the heat shield, which reads as a saturated bright spot. HiRISE interprets that brightness as a specular reflection and infers from it that the shield's dark outer face is turned downwards.

HiRISE cutout of China's Tianwen-1 landing site in southern Utopia Planitia, imaged on 6 June 2021, three weeks after the 14 May landing. The lander sits inside a dark blast pattern with the Zhurong rover a short distance to the south, and a bright piece of discarded entry hardware appears at lower left; HiRISE identifies the parachute with its back shell and the heat shield separately in the same observation.

Perseverance's back shell, left of centre, and its supersonic parachute at right, photographed from 8 m above the ground by the Ingenuity helicopter on its 26th flight on 19 April 2022, at the request of the Mars Sample Return team. The pair hit the ground at about 126 km/h after being jettisoned at 2.1 km altitude.
